title: Cornish Pasty
subtitle: Short-crust pastry crimped around raw beef skirt, potato, swede, and onion
excerpt: A Cornish pasty is raw beef skirt, potato, swede, and onion sealed inside a shortcrust pastry case with the crimp along the top and baked until the filling steams to tenderness. The filling goes in raw and cooks inside the pastry, which gives a different, more concentrated result than a pre-cooked filling.
sourceNotes: The Cornish pasty has Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) status in the EU and UK. The authentic filling is raw beef skirt, potato, swede, and onion, with the crimp along the top edge rather than the side. Traditional recipe shape adapted from Cornish food heritage sources.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze unbaked pasties on a tray, then bag once solid. Bake from frozen at 180°C for 55 to 60 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Scale the filling in exact proportion. Pastry can be made in a double or triple batch and refrigerated for up to 3 days.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Assemble pasties up to 24 hours ahead and refrigerate on a lined tray. Brush with egg wash just before baking.
recipe.temperatureNote: fan oven, reduce to 160°C fan after 20 minutes

glossaryTerms.definition: Folding and pressing the pastry edge to create a sealed, decorative border. On a Cornish pasty, the crimp runs along the top rather than the side.

content.text: A Cornish pasty is raw filling baked inside shortcrust pastry: the beef, potato, swede, and onion go in uncooked and steam to tenderness in the sealed case. The result is more savoury and concentrated than a pasty made with cooked filling. The
runs along the top edge: that is the authentic Cornish shape, not the side. Watch the oven temperature: the pasty starts hot to set the pastry, then drops to let the filling cook through gently.

Put the flour and salt in a large bowl. Add the cold butter and lard and rub in quickly with your fingertips until the mixture resembles coarse breadcrumbs. Add the cold water a little at a time, mixing with a table knife until the dough just comes together. Do not add more water than needed.
Press into a disc, wrap in cling film, and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Cold pastry is much easier to handle and holds its shape during crimping.
Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Divide the pastry into 4 equal pieces. Roll each to a rough circle about 25 cm in diameter, 3 to 4 mm thick.

Layer the filling across one half of each pastry circle, leaving a 2 cm border: potato first, then swede, then onion, then beef. Season each layer well with salt and pepper. Dot a little butter over the top.

Moisten the pastry border with water. Fold the plain half of the pastry over the filling to form a half-moon. Press the edges firmly together. Starting at one end, crimp by folding and twisting the edge in a rope pattern: this is the traditional top crimp, which runs along the curved edge.

Place on a lined baking tray. Brush all over with beaten egg. Cut a small steam vent near the crimp. Bake at 200°C fan for 20 minutes until the pastry is set and beginning to colour, then reduce the oven to 160°C fan and bake for a further 35 minutes. The filling cooks by steam in this lower phase.

items.cause: Pastry was too cold and dry, or rolled too thin
items.fix: Bring the pastry out of the fridge for 5 minutes before rolling. Aim for 3 to 4 mm thickness: any thinner and the pastry cracks at the folds.

items.cause: The oven temperature was kept too high throughout, setting the pastry quickly but not conducting enough heat to cook the raw filling through
items.fix: The two-stage method is essential. If the filling still feels firm, add 10 more minutes at 160°C. A very thick potato or swede slice is the usual culprit: keep slices under 3 mm.

items.symptom: Pastry is soggy at the base
items.fix: Dry the swede and potato slices on kitchen paper after cutting. Do not add any stock or liquid: the raw filling creates its own steam.

items.cause: The join was not sealed firmly enough before baking
items.fix: Press the edges firmly before crimping. If crimping is new, a fork seal along the edge works as a backup: less traditional but secure.

content.text: The Cornish pasty is a working food in origin: miners and farm labourers in Cornwall carried them as packed lunches, the thick crimped edge functioning as a handle so hands soiled with tin ore could grip and eat without touching the food. The crimp was thrown away. Each end was sometimes filled differently: meat one end, apple jam the other: though this is disputed by some Cornish food historians. The pasty has PGI status, meaning only pasties made in Cornwall following the traditional recipe can be sold as 'Cornish pasties'.
